technical_facts: Portability in games is defined by the ability to display output and receive platform-specific inputs.
The four primary inputs to a game are keystrokes, mouse moves, network packets, and time.
In Quake 2, inputs were handled in separate locations (e.g., Sys_SendKeyEvents() for keys/mouse, separate network system checks, and Sys_Milliseconds() calls throughout the code).
For Quake 3, Carmack implemented a single system event queue to unify all forms of input, similar to the Windows message queue.
A journaling system was created to record all inputs from the system event queue.
Journaling of time and inputs converts a real-time application into a batch process for debugging and quality control.
This approach allows for accurate session restarts, conditional breakpoints on frame numbers, and playback at degraded speeds without changing code paths.
Commander Keen 1 featured an adaptive play rate based on frame speed to prevent the game from becoming unplayable on faster computers.
personality_patterns: Struggles with the pressure of writing detailed .plan updates due to the fear of being misinterpreted or overwhelmed by follow-up emails.
Prefers terse comments but recognizes they are often misinterpreted.
Self-reflective and critical of his own past technical decisions (e.g., admitting he 'slipped' on portability in Q2).
Deeply focused on the intersection of time and input/output in real-time applications.
Values clarity and the 'aha' moment when a problem is seen clearly in its entirety.

gnosis_principles.description: Combining all external inputs (including time) into a single event queue simplifies the system architecture and enables advanced debugging tools like journaling.
By journaling all inputs and time, a real-time interactive application can be treated as a batch process, eliminating non-determinism and enabling precise debugging of transient flaws.
Viewing time as an explicit input value rather than a system property allows for deterministic playback and simulation control.

heritage_patterns: Cross-developing from NEXTSTEP to ensure portability across platforms.
Defining clear system interfaces to separate game logic from platform-specific code.

dpo_pairs.prompt: What was the primary technical change Carmack made for Quake 3's input system?
dpo_pairs.chosen: He unified all forms of input—keystrokes, mouse moves, network packets, and time—into a single system event queue, similar to the Windows message queue.
dpo_pairs.rejected: He created a new system for handling keystrokes and mouse movements to make the game more than just a portable game.
